sources.news_title: JUST IN: “Court Blocks Unlawful Construction of Triumphal Arch”
sources.text:
From The Committee of 100 on the Federal City (C100):
“Today, a federal judge in Washington, D.C. issued a temporary restraining order blocking the Trump administration from starting unlawful construction of the Triumphal Arch for fourteen days, at the entrance of Arlington National Cemetery. As part of that ruling, the judge found that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their claim that Congressional approval is necessary before constructing a memorial on public lands that belong to all Americans.
This emergency relief was granted in Lemmon v. Trump, which consolidated lawsuits brought by Public Citizen on behalf of three Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian, and by the Commonwealth of Virginia and Washington DC. National Parks Conservation Association (NPCA ) joined groups of advocacy, conservation and historic preservation organizations to submit a friend of the court brief in support of stopping construction. The groups are NPCA, the Coalition to Protect America’s National Parks, the National Trust for Historic Preservation, The Cultural Landscape Foundation, the Committee of 100 on the Federal City, DC Preservation League, and the American Institute of Architects.
The groups argue that the Trump administration’s failure to comply with numerous federal laws will have significant and permanent consequences for the National Mall, Arlington National Cemetery, and the surrounding national park landscape. At more than 250 feet, it would stand more than twice the height of the Lincoln Memorial, disrupt the historic connection to Arlington National Cemetery and permanently desecrate the viewshed of the National Mall. The location, design, and scale of the proposed Arch threaten the deliberate and historic design of the Capital’s monumental core and will unlawfully encroach on hundreds of thousands of service members and their families laid to rest here, and more than 40 historic properties. The groups are represented by O’Melveny & Myers LLP and Cultural Heritage Partners.
The groups celebrated the news by stating:
“This fight is not just about halting a massive and inappropriate intrusion into a sacred American cultural landscape,” said Judy Chesser, chair of the Committee of 100 on the Federal City. “It is also about stopping the Administration’s anti-democratic effort to remake the nation’s Capital without the engagement of Congress and the public. This ruling stands for something very simple: it is about respecting the rule of law.” Chesser’s full statement can be found on the Committee of 100 website.
“We are grateful that the court has paused the construction of this egregious arch,” said Jimi Shaughnessy, USMC and NPCA Veterans Program Manager. “Collectively, hundreds of thousands of Americans have voiced their concerns about the lack of congressional approval, box check public process and the lack of meaning or purpose, size, scope and cost of this unlawful project. Today is a small win and we are determined to ensure this arch never gets built here.“
“For nearly a century, the extraordinary landscape connecting the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery has told a powerful story about American sacrifice, reconciliation, and national unity,” said Brent Leggs, President and CEO of the National Trust for Historic Preservation. “We applaud the court’s decision to protect this sacred landscape from a massive and deeply inappropriate construction project that would permanently undermine its historic meaning.”
“The administration is learning they cannot ignore the judiciary in the way they’ve ignored the public throughout the review process at the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts and the National Capital Planning Commission, and by abruptly terminating Section 106 consultation, where “the views of the public are essential to informed Federal decision making,” said Charles A. Birnbaum, Founding President & CEO of The Cultural Landscape Foundation – a Washington, D.C. based education and advocacy organization.
“The view from the Lincoln Memorial across the river to Arlington National Cemetery was designed to tie the nation’s sacrifice to its promise. It is not a place for a president to build a monument to himself,“ said Emily Thompson, Executive Director of the Coalition to Protect America’s National Parks. “Today’s ruling affirms what we know to be true: these lands belong to all Americans, and no president gets to reshape them without Congress and the public having a say. Placing a structure twice the height of the Lincoln Memorial on the doorstep of Arlington National Cemetery would permanently scar a landscape that hundreds of thousands of service members and their families rest within. Once built, it can’t be undone, and the court was right to stop it before it starts.”

The legal challenge was brought by Washington, D.C., and Virginia, which argued that construction could create significant traffic disruptions, public safety concerns and financial burdens for their governments. In her 33-page opinion, Chutkan agreed that the local governments had demonstrated a likelihood of success on their legal claims and faced the possibility of immediate, irreparable harm if construction moved forward.
The judge also questioned the administration’s reliance on national security as a justification for the project. Many argued that placing such a massive structure near Arlington National Cemetery would undermine the solemn character of the area and alter an important historic landscape.
Supporters, including members of the federal planning commission appointed by Trump, defended the arch as a monument honoring the country and its military history.

For residents of the Washington metropolitan area, the dispute involves more than a proposed monument. The construction could affect traffic around one of the region’s most heavily traveled corridors, with potential consequences for commuters, emergency responders and visitors traveling between Washington and Northern Virginia.

sources.news_title: Federal Judge Delivers Major Blow to Trump’s Controversial Triumphal Arch in Washington
sources.text:
A federal judge has temporarily stopped the Trump administration from beginning construction of President Donald Trump’s proposed 250-foot Triumphal Arch in Washington, delivering a major legal setback to the controversial project.
Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a 14-day temporary restraining order on Thursday night, prohibiting the government from undertaking any construction-related activities while the legal dispute continues.
The decision came just hours after the administration announced that work on the proposed monument could begin immediately.
The ruling has placed the project’s construction schedule in uncertainty, despite plans for a three-year development period.
Federal Commission Approves the Monument
Earlier on Thursday, the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC), the federal agency responsible for overseeing major construction and development projects in Washington, voted 8-4 to approve the proposed structure.
The decision followed nearly nine hours of public testimony, during which administration representatives defended the project and said construction could begin within 24 hours.
The approval highlighted divisions between Trump’s allies and local officials, with supporters largely drawn from the administration and individuals closely connected to the president.
Opposition came from members of Congress, veterans, architects and residents of Washington, DC, and Virginia, many of whom raised objections to the monument’s proposed design and location.
California Democratic Representative Jared Huffman was among the most outspoken critics.
Speaking at the commission hearing, Huffman said Trump was a president rather than a king and described the proposed monument as an inappropriate development for the area.
Monument Could Cost Up to $100 Million
The proposed arch is expected to stand near Arlington National Cemetery, reaching approximately 250 feet into the air, equivalent to a 25-storey building.
Although the administration has not announced a final construction budget or explained how the project would be financed, estimates have placed its potential cost at up to $100 million.
The monument, which Trump has referred to as the Arc de Trump, has faced opposition over its proposed scale, appearance and location.
Huffman described the project as an illegal development and criticised its potential effect on the historic surroundings.
He also argued that the structure would disrespect veterans and the history and aesthetics of the area.
Judge Questions Administration’s Security Justification
Chutkan’s intervention followed earlier concerns about the administration’s attempts to accelerate the project while legal proceedings remained unresolved.
The judge had previously instructed the government to notify her before beginning construction, giving her an opportunity to intervene.
Trump introduced a new justification for the project late last month, announcing that the proposed arch would also serve as a military facility.
In a statement published on Truth Social, he said the structure would accommodate drones and ammunition for rapid deployment in large quantities.
He also described plans for rooftop and plaza positions that could accommodate sniper teams.
Trump said the monument, planned near the Arlington Memorial Bridge, would become a major military complex as well as a triumphal arch.
He argued that Washington was the only one among 59 major cities and capitals without such a monument and declared that the proposed structure would be the greatest of its kind.
However, Judge Chutkan questioned the administration’s explanation in her latest ruling.
Although she acknowledged the government’s interest in national security, she said the newly presented military functions were not supported by the original planning documents.
She also noted that the security features had not appeared in the documents used to review and approve the project, despite discussions about the structure having continued for approximately a year.
Democrats Threaten to Scrap the Project
The legal challenge comes as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress in January following their victories in Tuesday’s midterm elections.
Party members have indicated that they intend to stop the proposed monument from proceeding once they assume control.
Huffman had already warned that the political support behind the project would disappear, declaring that the Great Gatsby party was over.
He also described the arch as a monstrosity and an unacceptable tribute at a site associated with military history and veterans.
The change in congressional leadership could create another obstacle for the administration as it attempts to secure the project’s future.
Trump’s White House Construction Plans Face Other Legal Challenges
The proposed arch is not the only major architectural project pursued by Trump during his second term to face legal scrutiny.
His planned White House ballroom has also attracted legal challenges, although elements of the development have continued, with funding allocated through the Secret Service budget.
Some aspects of that project remain caught up in lawsuits.
With Chutkan’s latest order preventing construction-related activities on the Triumphal Arch for 14 days, the administration must now contend with the ongoing legal proceedings before work can move forward.

Trump’s Washington Triumph Arch Blocked by Federal Judge
The 76-meter monument cleared a key federal review, but a court has halted construction for two weeks as legal challenges question whether the president can move ahead without congressional approval
President Donald Trump’s plan to build a monumental triumphal arch in Washington has hit a legal barrier. A federal judge has temporarily barred his administration from starting construction, putting the 76-meter project on hold just hours after a key government commission voted to approve it.
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan ordered the two-week suspension overnight, giving the court time to review legal challenges to the project. The ruling prevents the administration from moving ahead with construction while the questions over its legality are examined.
The timing underscored the conflict surrounding the proposed monument. Late yesterday, the National Capital Planning Commission — one of two federal agencies responsible for overseeing architectural and design changes in Washington — had voted 8 to 4 to approve the project. That decision, however, did not end the opposition or resolve the legal questions now before the court.
More than 100 people representing a range of organizations addressed the commission during a hearing that continued late into the evening. Opposition to the arch was overwhelmingly critical, with speakers challenging both its symbolism and the legal basis for its construction.
Rep. Jared Huffman, the leading Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, which has jurisdiction over public parks, opened the public comments with a direct warning.
“This arch would dishonor America, our ideals and our laws,” Huffman said. He also cautioned that contractors working on the project could expose themselves to legal violations, urging public officials and companies involved to consider the consequences before proceeding.
“I urge all officials and companies involved in this illegal project to think about the legal risks they could face by carrying it forward,” he said.
Huffman closed with a pointed reference to the approaching change in Congress: “In case you haven’t heard, we will soon have a new Congress that takes the rule of law very seriously.”
The legal opposition extends beyond the objections raised at the commission hearing. Several veterans have filed a lawsuit seeking to stop construction, arguing that federal law requires congressional approval for the project. The attorneys general of Washington, D.C., and Virginia have also filed challenges this week.
The judge’s order now gives those challenges a critical window for judicial review. Despite the commission’s approval, Trump’s administration cannot begin building the arch during the two-week pause.

sources.news_title: US Judge Temporarily Blocks Trump’s Triumphal Arch In Washington
sources.text:
A judge temporarily blocked construction from beginning on President Donald Trump’s proposed 250-foot (76-meter) triumphal arch in Washington late on Thursday, shortly after it won a key approval.
US District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a 14-day restraining order following the National Capital Planning Commission 8-4 vote to approve the project after it heard from about 100 opponents, including Democratic lawmakers.
The Trump administration contends Congress approved the arch more than 100 years ago when it also authorized construction of a bridge across the Potomac River.
Disruption Of Traffic
“The sheer improbability that a 100-year-old statute would contain authority, unknown to every previous administration, to erect a 250-foot arch at a principal location in the nation’s capital indicates how far (the government) must stretch to justify this project,” Chutkan wrote.
She said approval would result in construction for about three years “that will disrupt traffic, create noise, result in large-scale excavation, and more.”
The Justice Department had said earlier that if the project had been approved it expected an initial six to eight months of construction focused on excavation and foundation work could begin as soon as Thursday. Above-ground construction would start in May 2027 at the earliest, with the job expected to take 33 to 39 months total.
“It will snarl traffic for years, impact the nearby airport, and present even more serious threats to public safety that this commission has refused to acknowledge and grapple with,” said Representative Don Beyer, a Democrat who represents northern Virginia.
The National Park Service also said late on Thursday it had approved the project.
‘Legally Indefensible’
The arch is among several costly projects Trump is pushing in Washington despite opposition from local officials and conservationists. They include rebuilding the Reflecting Pool at the Lincoln Memorial, constructing a massive White House ballroom and overhauling the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.
The arch has faced significant opposition in the courts. The state of Virginia and the District of Columbia sued the National Park Service and the Department of the Interior on Saturday, seeking to halt the start of construction, calling it “legally indefensible” and arguing that Congress has not approved it.
They also raised a number of concerns about the project’s impact on traffic
At an event on Monday to highlight improvements to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, Trump said the arch would also serve as a military asset and would be able to house drones and snipers.
“It’s right smack in the middle of everything, so very important for our military. But from a beautification standpoint, it’ll be the most beautiful arch in the world,” Trump said.
Inspiration From Paris?
The arch, which would include an eternal flame and floodlights to make it visible to pilots, would be situated across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial on a highway roundabout near the entrance to Arlington National Cemetery.
It would resemble the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, but stand more than 80 feet taller. It would also be nearly as tall as the US Capitol, which at 288 feet, can be seen across much of Washington. The site is near airplanes’ final approach to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport.
A rendering showed the flame would be held by a 60-foot-tall gold, winged female figure positioned atop the arch and flanked by gold flying eagles.
Critics say it would place some graves at Arlington National Cemetery in shadow, while the Trump administration said it would honor veterans.

sources.text:
Trump’s Proposed Triumphal Arch Blocked by Federal Judge
A US federal judge has temporarily halted construction of Trump's proposed 250-foot triumphal arch amid legal challenges from veterans and local authorities.
The ruling came hours after the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) voted 8-4 to approve the final plans for the proposed monument. The decision followed nearly nine hours of public comments from lawmakers, veterans, architects and residents of Washington, DC, and Virginia.
The commission serves as the federal government’s planning authority for the region. Its approval had cleared a major planning hurdle for the project, which is intended to mark 250 years of American independence.
However, the court order has temporarily prevented the administration from moving ahead with construction. The Justice Department had previously told the court that work could begin as early as Thursday.
In a court filing on Wednesday night, the administration also disclosed that a construction company “may be — but is not necessarily — arranging off-site preparations for construction mobilization in anticipation of permit approval” at the location.
Before the commission’s vote, its executive director, Mark Paoletta, recommended approving the proposed site and building plans. Paoletta, who also serves as the top lawyer at the Office of Management and Budget, praised Trump’s plans and described the structure as the “grandest arch ever built by mankind.”
However, the proposal faced strong opposition during the public hearing. California Congressman Jared Huffman, the leading Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, described the project as “illegal” and warned that it could “disrupt the solemn connection” between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.
“This arch would dishonor America, our ideals, and our laws,” Huffman told the commission. He also argued that Congress, rather than the administration, should lead discussions about building such a monument.
Marine veteran Jimi Shaughnessy also criticised the proposal, raising concerns about its potential impact on the area and its significance to military families.
“a dominating arch with a carnival-like atmosphere of tourists, food trucks and buses is abhorrent and insulting to those who gave all and to their families,” he said.
He further questioned the administration’s spending priorities, saying it should focus on challenges facing military families rather than using public money to develop a monument that had not been requested.
The proposed 250-foot monument will have a main structure measuring 166 feet, topped by three gilded figures. These will include a golden winged female figure with a golden eagle flying on either side.
According to documents submitted to the planning commission, the monument will stand at Memorial Circle, between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, across the Potomac River.
The structure will also include an observation deck. The administration estimates that it could attract between 2,000 and 22,400 visitors daily.
Although the Triumphal Arch project is expected to take three years to complete, questions remain about its overall cost and who will pay for it.
The monument will also stand close to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. The Federal Aviation Administration has determined that it will pose “no hazard to air navigation”, subject to safety requirements involving lighting. These include a non-standard eternal flame and continuous floodlighting.
Trump previously described the proposed arch in September as a “top grade Military Complex” that would house drones and sniper ammunition. However, the documents submitted to the NCPC do not mention these military uses.
During an October court hearing, Justice Department lawyers declined to provide further details about the proposed national security features.
The planning commission received more than 1,300 public comments about the project, with most expressing opposition.
Meanwhile, the legal battle over the monument continues. Vietnam War veterans and local authorities have filed separate lawsuits arguing that the administration cannot proceed without congressional approval and must follow the legal procedures required for major construction projects.
In an earlier order on Tuesday, Judge Chutkan instructed the government to notify her within one hour of the commission’s decision. She also required 30 minutes’ notice before any preparations for construction began, allowing her time to consider whether to stop the work.
After receiving the government’s notice late Thursday, she issued the temporary restraining order.
During an earlier hearing, Chutkan identified the veterans’ legal right to bring the case as one of the most important questions before her. The issue is known as legal standing, which determines whether a person or group has sufficient grounds to challenge a government action in court.
The Supreme Court had earlier ruled that plaintiffs seeking to stop construction of a White House ballroom were unlikely to have the legal standing required to challenge that project.
The Justice Department has urged Chutkan to apply the same reasoning to the arch dispute. Its lawyers described the plaintiffs’ applications as “breathless”.
However, attorneys representing the veterans and local governments argue that their legal claims differ from those raised in the ballroom case.
Two veterans involved in the lawsuit, Michael Lemmon and Shaun Byrnes, told the court that the proposed monument would affect their experience when visiting graves at Arlington National Cemetery. They also raised concerns about the structure’s enormous size and purpose.
Virginia and Washington, DC, filed a separate lawsuit in late October, which was also assigned to Chutkan.
Their attorneys general warned that construction could cause lasting damage to both jurisdictions.
“as soon as Defendants break ground on this project, they will inflict irreparable harm” they argued, adding that “the Arch project will inevitably snarl traffic between the jurisdictions, produce pollution and stormwater runoff in the Potomac, interfere with emergency services, and pose numerous other challenges.”
For now, the judge’s 14-day order prevents the administration from starting construction-related work at the site while the legal proceedings continue.

Judge blocks Trump arch hours after federal panel approval
A federal judge temporarily blocked President Donald Trump’s proposed “triumphal arch” in Washington, D.C., just hours after a federal panel voted to give final approval to the project Thursday night.
D.C. District Court Judge Tonya S. Chutkan granted the D.C. and Virginia governments’ request for a temporary restraining order late Thursday, halting the Trump administration’s efforts to begin construction for at least 14 days.
Chutkan also consolidated the case with a separate lawsuit filed by three Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian.
The vote by the National Capital Planning Commission, which is led by Trump appointees, was 8-4. The vote came after hours of public testimony, including from the Vietnam veteran who's leading the lawsuit to stop the project, who called it "frankly blasphemous."
Michael Lemmon, who served in the Army before spending a career in the foreign service, told the NCPC that the 250-foot arch would "profoundly disturb the peace and tranquility" owed to those buried at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.
"It is frankly blasphemous," Lemmon told the commission.
Lemmon was one of some 130 people who had signed up to provide their comments to the NCPC before its final vote.
The proposed arch would be more than twice as tall as the 99-foot-high Lincoln Memorial and taller than France's Arc de Triomphe.
The public testimony began with a fiery exchange between Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the top Democrat on the House Natural Resources Committee, and NCPC Chair Mark Paoletta.
Huffman blasted plans for the arch, saying it "would dishonor America, our ideals and our laws."
Paoletta challenged Huffman on his knowledge of the history of Columbia Island -- where the arch would be built across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial -- insisting the project was authorized over 100 years ago when Congress approved the initial plan for Memorial Bridge, which connects Washington, D.C., with the cemetery.
"If you want to make that argument to a federal court, go for it. You're going to lose," Huffman responded.
A lawsuit filed by Lemmon and fellow vets, recently joined by D.C. and Virginia, accuses the Trump administration of violating federal law by not seeking specific congressional authorization for the project.
Paoletta, a Trump loyalist who also serves as OMB's general counsel and acting head of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, defended the arch at the start of the meeting.
"President Trump's historic vision for a monumental arch at Memorial Circle would complete a project over a century in the making," Paoletta said, adding that the project would "honor our nation and her veterans, and provide the sacred ground of Arlington National Cemetery with the monumental gateway it deserves."
Pointing to President Trump's plan to have the arch house drones, snipers and ammunition, Paoletta also said the arch would mark "a generational security opportunity to protect our nation's capital."
With the administration indicating it could begin construction as soon as the NCPC grants its final approval, the judge presiding over the lawsuit against the project has ordered the administration to provide the court with at least 30 minutes' notice before any work begins.
Earlier Thursday, the Justice Department informed the court that a construction contractor had prematurely painted lines on the grounds. Pictures of the painted grass were posted by a freelance photographer.
Lawyers for the administration say the contractor "did not have authorization from the National Park Service (NPS) to undertake the line painting," adding that NPS officials might "periodically visit the site to prevent unauthorized activity."
The Park Service plans to have construction of the arch take place 20 hours per day over the next two to three years, according to planning documents released earlier this year by the Interior Department.
